sentences: In July 1830, Parisians overthrew their king, Charles X, in three days of revolution.
Eugène Delacroix painted this huge canvas that very same year.
Stand back for a moment: we are facing a smoking barricade.
That October, Delacroix wrote to his brother that he had taken on a modern subject, a barricade.
If he had not fought for his country, he added, at least he would paint for her.
He was already the leading painter of French Romanticism.
The woman raising the tricolor flag is not a real person but an allegory of Liberty herself.
Her red cap is the Phrygian cap, a symbol of freedom since the Revolution of 1789.
She is also seen as Marianne, the emblem of the French Republic.
On the left, a worker with a raised sabre advances beside a bourgeois in a top hat, gripping his gun.
Many names have been suggested for the top-hatted man, but no one knows for sure.
What matters is that different classes march in one line.
At Liberty's feet, a wounded man kneels and lifts his eyes to her.
His blue jacket, red sash and white shirt repeat the three colours of the flag.
Those three colours echo all across the canvas.
To Liberty's right, a boy charges forward shouting, a pistol in each hand.
He stands for the working people of the city.
He is often linked to Gavroche, the street urchin in Victor Hugo's later novel Les Misérables.
Far off to the right, the towers of Notre-Dame rise through the smoke.
Look carefully and you can spot a tiny tricolor flying from them.
It is a reminder that this is not a myth but a real day in Paris.
The bodies at their feet make no secret of revolution's cost.
On the left lies a half-stripped man; on the right, a soldier in uniform.
This heap of rubble and corpses becomes the pedestal from which Liberty strides forward.
The whole composition rises like a pyramid toward the flag at its peak.
Delacroix favoured free brushwork and colour over precise outlines.
That choice set Romanticism apart from the academic taste for careful drawing.
The painting was first shown at the Salon of 1831, and the French government bought it for 3,000 francs.
Its political message was so strong that it was taken off view within months.
Only in 1874 did it enter the Louvre for good.
Finally, step back and look at Liberty's face.
Even as she strides ahead, she turns her head to call the people behind her.
Standing before this barricade, you might ask yourself where in the crowd you would be.
